_about: The dashboard To-Do feed. Refreshed at every Rule 8 checkpoint alongside the session handoff — this is the handoff distilled into plain language for the 📋 button on every tab. Split For Sam (curation / decisions only a human makes) and For Fable (engineering, the next session picks up).
_as_of: 2026-08-24 · Session 188 went back over the ESL fold and checked it against something nobody had read: the colleges' own catalog descriptions. The tool that sorted ESL into Beginning/Intermediate/Advanced only ever looked at course TITLES — but the course catalog we already hold describes 96% of these courses in plain English, and those descriptions often say the level outright. The very first course in the pile we had called 'impossible to check' says 'at the advanced ESL level' in both of its college descriptions, and we had filed it as Beginning. Checking all 1,990 folds this way also told us which of our own rules to trust. The rule that reads a number in the title ('ESL 2', 'Level 5') and infers a level is wrong about half the time — because colleges run ladders of different lengths, so '2' is the bottom rung at one college and the middle rung at another. We had ranked that rule as the SAFER of the two piles and told the next session to look at it last. Separately, Sam deleted an old scheduled task that could have fought the daily dashboard update, and we confirmed the seven ESL courses have no other bad entries hiding inside them.
_status: The ESL fold has now been double-checked and two decisions are waiting on Sam. We found 222 courses where the college's own catalog disagrees with the level we filed them under. Nearly all of them we filed too LOW, which is the cautious direction and can be fixed slowly. But NINE we filed too HIGH — claiming more credit than the college describes — and those are the ones worth Sam's time first. All nine have the same cause: our rule treats 'level 5 and above' as Advanced, but several colleges run a six-rung ladder where 5 and 6 are still called high-intermediate. Six of the nine are the same Los Angeles district course series repeated across eight colleges. Nothing has been changed in the live data — these are proposals waiting for a decision.

items.text: Nine ESL courses are filed one level HIGHER than the college's own catalog describes them — the only ones running against the cautious direction, so they are worth your eye before the other 213. They all share a cause: our rule says 'level 5 or above = Advanced', but several colleges run a six-rung ladder where 5 and 6 are still 'high-intermediate'. Six of the nine are the same Los Angeles district series (College ESL V) repeated across eight colleges. Two ways to fix it: correct the nine by hand, or move the cut from '5 and above' to '6 and above', which fixes six of them by rule. Second question while you are here: that number rule is wrong about half the time overall — is it worth keeping at all? Full list and the quoted catalog text: kb/esl_fold_spotcheck/2026-08-24/report.md.

Try the whole-reference map: search for a subject, drag one subject next to another, and move a course between them. Tell us what is wrong with it — especially whether dragging a subject around is actually how you would want to work.

One row to look at: five different Orange Coast College courses — Reading and Vocabulary, Sentence Structure, Spelling, Pronunciation and Grammar — are filed as one course under the name of just one of them. About 3,320 rows share that shape.

Add the over-merge detector to the auditor: flag any course row where every college listed is the same college but the course numbers differ. 3,320 rows qualify. Flag only, never un-merge automatically — some are legitimate.

Half the reference queue — 3,001 decisions covering 8,065 courses — has no subject assigned at all, so it cannot be merged until someone says what subject each belongs to. Different job, needs its own screen.

ESL proved packaging works. Pick the next discipline and repeat it — Kinesiology is the biggest at 1,204 course records, then Music and Computer Information Systems. Before ranking that discipline's queue, run the same catalog-description check ESL got and measure which of the sorting rules actually hold up — on ESL that reordered the work and found 94 rows that were about to be skipped (kb/_build_esl_fold_spotcheck.py is the pattern).

Settle the noncredit minimum — it is the last open number on the funding tab. At the $50,000 you set, 30 of the 33 noncredit institutions land exactly on it and an institution has to reach 3,909 noncredit FTES before growing earns it anything extra. At $25,000 it was 27 of 33 and 3,022 FTES. So the current setting rewards getting into the lane and pays very little for growing inside it. If that is what you want, nothing needs to change. If you wanted growth to pay, lowering the minimum is the lever — raising the set-aside on its own makes it more floor-bound, not less. The box on the tab and the explainer page both show the break-even figure live, so you can move the dial and watch it.

Your question about splitting P1 into three metrics (landing page, student portal, batch upload). Short answer: get the breakdown first, split later if the data says to. Splitting it into three priorities would split the MONEY three ways — each would get its own target and its own cap, so a college doing everything through its landing page could no longer make up the difference elsewhere. That is a real change: it would require colleges to work all three routes rather than reach one total. Also, batch upload is not really the same thing as the other two — those are students arriving, that is an administrative import — so it is the one worth treating differently whatever you decide. Recommendation: when the data lands next week we show the three origins as a breakdown on the existing P1, in the drill-in and the export. You then have the evidence, and splitting later is a settings change, not a rebuild.

Move Sierra's Anthropic billing to the corporate account when you can. She went dark twice in two days on the personal balance — 2026-08-21 and again overnight — and each outage takes down every place she appears at once: the public page, the COBI tab, the Fact Sheet drawer, map.rccd.edu, the college landing pages and the vendor iframe. A student who arrives in that window gets nothing and files no complaint, so the outage cannot report itself. There is now an automatic check every three hours that will open a GitHub issue and close it on recovery, so you will hear about the next one — but it tells you after the fact, it does not prevent it.

Trial Haiku 4.5 against the smoke suite. It is a third of Sonnet's price both directions and stacks with the caching we just shipped rather than competing with it. ONE of the two concerns is now closed: her biggest measured question used about 23,000 tokens against Haiku's 200,000 limit, a 9x margin, so capacity is not the obstacle — that came free from the deploy telemetry. What is left is only whether a smaller model keeps the careful bits: the 'not every recommendation should be applied' caveat, 'showing 9 of 261' rather than implying that is all of them, not calling an absent college zero. Several smoke assertions test exactly those. Run it, diff the failures, report — do not switch quietly.

MAP needs to give us two college IDs. You ruled that Calbright and LAUNCH each have two entities — one credit, one noncredit. The noncredit halves already have IDs; the credit halves ("Calbright College Credit" and "Launch Apprenticeship Non-Credit") have none anywhere we can see, and MAP is the only system allowed to assign one. We deliberately did NOT make one up, because a fake ID would look exactly like a real one to every other system. They show as "awaiting MAP ID" on the College Identity tab. Once MAP supplies them, they fold in with no code change.

The map can move a local course, but it cannot undo a wrong merge between two courses, and it cannot correct a subject label. Both are real: a film course is stuck inside the new Enrichment ESL course and there is no way to pull it out, and 73 merges between Ethnic Studies and Kinesiology are correct merges filed under the wrong subject. Neither is fixable from any screen we have. Still blocked for the film-course example: a merged-away course does not appear on the map at all, so there is nothing to drag.

Finish ESL: 67 ESL records were never in the fold's candidate list at all, because they live in a different store (the Z-scheme rows from the 2026-06 renumbering) rather than the two files the packaging tool reads. They are the concrete remaining ESL job — not a vague 'second pass'. Same survivors, same method.
